external-call.title: A call that leaves the process: HTTP, SDK, database, queue, cache server
external-call.read: The enclosing function, every caller up to an entry point, and the construction of the client it uses. For a client or SDK default such as a retry count, read the installed library source and cite it.

questions.text: Does a successful call change state outside the process?
questions.yes: It creates, updates, deletes, sends, publishes, enqueues, starts, charges or invokes. Name the effect.
questions.no: It only reads: get, list, describe, a query without side effects.

questions.text: Does the request carry a caller-chosen key that the provider uses to deduplicate repeats?
questions.yes: An idempotency key, client token, deterministic resource or execution name, or a conditional-write precondition. Name the field.
questions.no: No such field, or a field the provider does not deduplicate on.

questions.text: Is that key derived from persisted or deterministic input, so a repeat from a new process sends the same key?
questions.yes: Derived from stored state, the request's own identity, or a deterministic name.
questions.no: Generated per attempt or per process: a random UUID, a timestamp, a counter.

questions.text: Is the call bounded by a deadline?
questions.yes: An abort signal, a client timeout option, or an enclosing timeout that interrupts it. Cite the bound and its value.
questions.no: Nothing bounds it short of the platform killing the process.

questions.text: Is a failed call repeated automatically anywhere?
questions.yes: A loop, recursion, a client or SDK default, a wrapper, a schedule, or the platform re-delivering the event. Cite each retry owner, including library defaults.
questions.no: Every owner was checked and none repeats it.

questions.text: Is it repeated by more than one of those owners?
questions.yes: Two or more owners. Name them.
questions.no: Exactly one owner.

questions.text: Is the repetition hand-written: a loop or recursion with a sleep or timer?
questions.no: A library, schedule or platform repeats it.

questions.text: Is the deadline outside the repetition, so it bounds every attempt and the waits between them?
questions.no: Only each attempt is bounded, or nothing bounds the whole.

questions.text: Before deciding the next action, does the code distinguish failures by kind?
questions.yes: Throttled, temporary, rejected and unknown-outcome failures take different paths. Cite the classifier.
questions.no: All failures take one path.

questions.text: After a failure that leaves the outcome unknown, does the code check whether the change happened before repeating it?
questions.yes: A timeout, dropped connection or 5xx on a change leads to a lookup. Cite the lookup.
questions.no: It repeats or gives up without looking.

questions.text: Does a failure reach the caller as a value that names the operation and keeps the original cause?
questions.yes: A typed error or tagged value with the operation and cause.
questions.no: A generic error, a string, a provider error with no operation name, or nothing.

questions.text: Is the call recorded in a span or a structured log with its operation name and outcome?
questions.no: No record, or a free-text message only.

questions.text: Is the response validated against a schema before its fields are used?
questions.no: Fields are read from an unvalidated or cast value. Answer n/a only when the response is unused.

questions.text: Is the call made inside an open database transaction?
questions.no: No transaction encloses it.

questions.text: Does the retry read a wait hint from the failed response, such as a Retry-After header or a provider's retry field?
questions.yes: Cite where the hint is read and used as the delay.
questions.no: The retry delay never reads the response.

questions.text: Is the call made through a project wrapper that already supplies the deadline, the typed failure and the record?
questions.no: The call is made directly, or through a wrapper missing one of the three.

import.title: An import of a client for an external system: network, storage, database, queue, process or file system
import.read: The import, the file's exports, and the other files that import the same module.

questions.text: Does another file import from the same module specifier?
questions.yes: Cite the other file's import line.
questions.no: No other file imports the specifier.

questions.text: Does a lint rule already restrict which files may import this module?
questions.no: No rule restricts it.

entry-point.title: Where work starts: a request handler, function handler, route, job, consumer or command
entry-point.read: The entry function, its middleware or wrapper, the platform configuration that triggers it (deployment templates, schedules, queue settings), and the work it starts.

questions.text: Are clients, layers, connections or other dependencies constructed inside the per-request or per-event function?
questions.yes: Cite the construction inside the function.
questions.no: They are built once per process, or there are none.

questions.text: Does the entry compute a deadline from the platform's remaining time or the request timeout and pass it to the work it starts?
questions.yes: Cite where it is computed and where it is passed.
questions.no: No deadline, or a fixed constant unrelated to the platform limit.

questions.text: Is every typed failure the work can produce mapped to a response or outcome by name?
questions.yes: Each failure kind has its own mapping; a generic fallback catches only defects.
questions.no: Some typed failures fall into a generic error response or a rethrow.

questions.text: Are request-scoped identifiers attached to every log and span emitted during the request?
questions.yes: A request, route, user or job id is set once and carried. Cite it.
questions.no: Logs carry none, or each site passes its own.

questions.text: Is the input validated against a schema before use?
questions.no: Fields are read from the raw event or a cast.

questions.text: Can the platform deliver the same event more than once?
questions.yes: Asynchronous invocation retries, an at-least-once queue, overlapping schedule ticks, or client retries. Cite the configuration in the repository.
questions.no: Delivery is at most once, and the configuration in the repository shows it.

questions.text: Does the entry check a dedupe record keyed by the event's identity before applying its effects?
questions.yes: Cite the record and the check.
questions.no: No dedupe record.

questions.text: Does the entry run Effect code?
questions.no: Plain promise or callback code.

questions.text: Is the Effect run through a runtime built once per process?
questions.yes: A module-level runtime, or one memoized layer build.
questions.no: Layers are provided inside each run.

config-read.title: A read of process configuration: environment variables and equivalents
config-read.read: The read, the helper that wraps it, every other read of the same key, and where the value is used.

questions.text: Is the value a secret: a password, token, key or credential?
questions.no: Not a secret.

questions.text: Is a missing or malformed value reported with the key's name before the value is used?
questions.no: A missing value becomes undefined, an empty string, NaN or a late failure without the key name.

questions.text: Is the value parsed by hand: number, boolean, JSON, list or enum?
questions.no: Used as a raw string.

questions.text: Is the same key read in another place?
questions.no: This is the only read.

questions.text: Can the value reach a log, error message, response or stored record?
questions.no: It is used only in requests to the service it authenticates or configures.

questions.text: Do tests set this key by mutating the global environment?
questions.no: Tests supply it another way or not at all.

error-definition.title: A definition of an error type
error-definition.read: The definition, every construction site, and every place that matches on it.

questions.text: Does the error carry a literal tag or discriminant that callers match on?
questions.no: Callers can tell it apart only by class or message.

questions.text: Does it keep the original cause?
questions.yes: A cause field or Error cause option.
questions.no: The cause is dropped or stringified.

questions.text: Is it written to storage, sent to another process or client, or embedded in a persisted record?
questions.no: It stays in memory.

questions.text: Does any caller distinguish it by message text?
questions.no: No caller matches on message text.

questions.text: Does another error type have the same fields?
questions.no: No other error type has the same fields.

error-handling.title: A place that catches or recovers from a failure
error-handling.read: The handler, the work it encloses, and what the caller receives after it runs.

questions.text: Does the handler end the failure without propagating it or returning a failure value?
questions.yes: It logs, returns a default, returns success or does nothing.
questions.no: It rethrows, fails, or returns a value that records the failure.

questions.text: Is the swallow marked as intended?
questions.yes: A named optional step, a comment that names the consequence, or an outcome value the caller reads.
questions.no: Nothing marks it.

questions.text: Does the handler catch interruption, abort or timeout failures along with ordinary failures?
questions.yes: It catches them in the same branch: Effect catchCause or ignoreCause without an interrupt check, or a catch-all around an abortable await.
questions.no: They pass through, or none can reach this handler.

questions.text: Does it replace the failure with a new one that drops the original cause?
questions.no: The cause survives.

questions.text: Does the handler run before a retry of the same work, so the retry never sees the failure?
questions.no: No retry follows, or the handler runs after it.

decode-boundary.title: Data entering typed code from outside: parse, cast, response body, stored record
decode-boundary.read: The source of the data, the decode or cast, and the first fields used.

questions.text: Does the data come from outside the process?
questions.yes: Network, storage, environment, user input, another service, or a file.
questions.no: It was produced in-process.

questions.text: Is it validated against a schema before any field is used?
questions.no: Fields are read first, or a hand-written guard checks only part of the shape.

questions.text: Is a type assertion applied to it?
questions.no: No cast.

questions.text: Does another place decode or cast external data to a type with the same field names?
questions.no: A search for the field names finds no other decode or cast of that shape.

questions.text: Does this codebase also write the same shape?
questions.no: Only read here.

questions.text: Does a decode failure produce a failure distinct from a transport or storage failure?
questions.no: It shares the transport failure's type, or throws a generic error.

state-write.title: A write to a store that outlives the request: database, object storage, key-value, file
state-write.read: The write, the read it depends on, every other writer of the same record, and any concurrency limit in the deployment configuration.

questions.text: Does another code path write the same table, key or file?
questions.no: A search for writes to the same table, key or file finds only this one.

questions.text: Is the write read-modify-write?
questions.yes: The written value is computed from a value read earlier.
questions.no: A blind write or an append.

questions.text: Is the write conditional on what was read?
questions.yes: A version, etag, if-absent, or WHERE on the read value. Cite it.
questions.no: Unconditional.

questions.text: If the write committed but the response was lost, can a retry recognize its own earlier write?
questions.yes: A writer id or version in the record lets it.
questions.no: A retry sees a conflict or a changed record and cannot tell why.

questions.text: Is the write paired with an external effect that must happen once per write?
questions.yes: A message, call or event. Cite it.
questions.no: No paired effect.

questions.text: Is the paired effect recorded in the same transaction or record for later delivery?
questions.yes: An outbox row or pending-effect field. Cite it.
questions.no: Performed separately; a crash between the two loses or repeats it.

pagination-loop.title: A loop that walks pages from an API or store
pagination-loop.read: The loop and each page request.

questions.text: Is the number of pages or items bounded?
questions.yes: A page cap, an item cap, or a provider limit. Cite it.
questions.no: Unbounded.

questions.text: Is each page request, or the whole loop, bounded by a deadline?
questions.no: No deadline.

questions.text: Is the same loop shape written in another place?
questions.no: Only here.

questions.text: Does the loop exit early or carry state between pages beyond the token?
questions.yes: Cite the early exit or state.
questions.no: It collects every page.

fan-out.title: Concurrent work over a collection
fan-out.read: The collection's source, the per-item work, and what the caller receives.

questions.text: Is the number of concurrent operations bounded?
questions.no: All items start at once.

questions.text: Is the item count set by external data?
questions.yes: Request input, stored rows, a listing.
questions.no: A fixed small set in code.

questions.text: Does each item's work run without reading another item's result?
questions.yes: No item reads another's result or relies on its success.
questions.no: Cite the dependency between items.

questions.text: Does one failure reject or abandon the rest?
questions.yes: Promise.all, Effect.all or forEach default mode.
questions.no: Every item runs to an outcome.

questions.text: Is each item's outcome reported to the caller or a log?
questions.no: Partial failures vanish.

questions.text: Does the provider offer a batch call for these items that is not used?
questions.no: No batch API, or it is used.

questions.text: Is Promise.race used with a timer to bound the work?
questions.no: Not a timer race.

time-read.title: A read of the clock or a timer
time-read.read: The read and the decision it feeds.

questions.text: Does the time feed a decision: a deadline, expiry, backoff, elapsed check or schedule?
questions.no: It only stamps a record or a log.

questions.text: Is that decision exercised by a test?
questions.no: No test reaches it.

questions.text: Does that test wait real time or patch the global clock?
questions.no: It injects time.

questions.text: Is wall-clock time subtracted to measure an elapsed duration?
questions.yes: Date values subtracted for a lease, timeout or rate decision. Cite it.
questions.no: Monotonic time is used, or no elapsed duration is measured.

log-site.title: A log statement
log-site.read: The statement and the values it includes.

questions.text: Is the record machine-parseable with a stable event name and fields?
questions.no: Free text, or an object the runtime prints in a non-parseable form.

questions.text: Does it carry the request, job or operation id?
questions.no: None.

questions.text: Can it include a secret, token or full user payload?
questions.no: Only identifiers and outcomes.

questions.text: Does it log a caught failure at a level below warning?
questions.yes: A failure from a catch block or error result logged at log, info or debug level.
questions.no: Logged at warning or error, or not a failure.

questions.text: Is this an Effect log call whose Effect is never run?
questions.yes: A bare statement in Effect code that is not yielded or returned.
questions.no: Yielded, returned, or not an Effect log.

resource.title: Something acquired that must be released: connection, handle, temporary file, timer, subscription, lock, launched instance
resource.read: The acquisition, every exit path of its owner, and the release.

questions.text: Is the resource released on every exit: success, failure, timeout and cancellation?
questions.no: Name the exit that skips it.

questions.text: Is it held across requests or for the process lifetime?
questions.no: Scoped to one request or call.

questions.text: Can two concurrent callers both reach the creation before either stores the result?
questions.yes: No guard between the check and the store.
questions.no: Guarded, or created once at startup.

questions.text: Is an AbortController built by hand to bound or cancel work?
questions.no: Not a hand-built controller.

module-state.title: Mutable state at module scope: caches, maps, singletons, counters
module-state.read: The declaration and every reader and writer.

questions.text: Is it a cache of values fetched or computed from elsewhere?
questions.no: Another kind of state.

questions.text: Does the cache have an expiry or size bound?
questions.no: Entries live forever.

questions.text: Do concurrent misses for the same key share one lookup?
questions.yes: An in-flight promise or lock is shared.
questions.no: Each miss starts its own lookup.

questions.text: Is a failed lookup stored as a value?
questions.yes: An empty or error result is cached.
questions.no: Failures are not stored.

questions.text: Can the cached source value change during the process lifetime?
questions.yes: A rotated secret, a changed configuration, an updated record. Cite the source.
questions.no: Fixed at build or startup.

questions.text: Is the state read, then an await happens, then the state is written from the earlier read?
questions.no: No await between read and dependent write.

background-work.title: Work started without the caller waiting for it
background-work.read: The started work, its owner, and what happens when the owner finishes or the process is frozen.

questions.text: Does the work write state, deliver a message or release a resource?
questions.no: It only records metrics, logs or warms a cache.

questions.text: Can the owner finish or the process freeze before the work completes?
questions.yes: A handler returns, a serverless runtime freezes, or a scope closes first.
questions.no: The owner waits for it or outlives it.

questions.text: Are its failures observed?
questions.yes: Logged or recorded with the operation name.
questions.no: A rejection or failure goes nowhere.

effect-boundary.title: Where Effect code is run or given its dependencies
effect-boundary.read: The run or provide call, the code around it, and the layer it uses.

questions.text: Is this run inside code that itself runs inside an Effect?
questions.yes: A nested run inside a generator, service method or callback of Effect code.
questions.no: At an outer edge.

questions.text: Is a layer provided here on every call, rather than once through a runtime?
questions.no: Provided once, or no layer.

questions.text: Does the boundary treat interruption and defects differently from typed failures?
questions.no: All three take one path.

questions.text: Is the run given the caller's cancellation signal or deadline?
questions.yes: A signal option, or a timeout derived from the caller.
questions.no: The run cannot be cancelled from outside.

questions.text: Is a request-scoped value captured when a layer is built and then shared by later requests?
questions.no: Request-scoped values are read per request.

test-double.title: A fake, mock or patched global in a test
test-double.read: The double, the code under test that receives it, and other test files' doubles of the same thing.

questions.text: Is an equivalent double defined in another test file?
questions.no: Only here.

questions.text: Does the test patch a global or a module export?
questions.yes: fetch, environment, console, the clock, or an imported module.
questions.no: The double is passed in.

questions.text: Does the code under test receive the double through a service, parameter or layer?
questions.no: Only through the patched global or module.

questions.text: Can the double inject failures, including a change that applies but whose response is lost?
questions.yes: Cite the failure modes it supports.
questions.no: Success only, or failure before applying only.

questions.text: Does the test wait real time?
questions.no: No waits, or injected time.

deadline.title: Deadline with interruption
deadline.note: A timeout inside a retry bounds one attempt. The whole deadline is an outer timeout. A timeout does not cancel work already accepted by the provider.

schedule-retry.title: Retry with a schedule
schedule-retry.note: Retry predicates go in Effect.retry({ schedule, while }). Schedule.jittered scales each delay by 0.8 to 1.2; full jitter needs modifyDelay. HttpClient.retryTransient retries regardless of method.

tagged-error.title: Tagged errors in the error channel
tagged-error.note: Callers match by tag; the compiler lists the failures a function can produce.

schema-error.title: Serializable tagged errors
schema-error.note: For errors written to storage or sent across a process.

schema-decode.title: Schema decode at the boundary
schema-decode.note: Decode once where data enters; do not decode again inside.

schema-class.title: Schema classes and brands for stored shapes
schema-class.note: One schema owns both reading and writing a stored shape.

config.title: Typed configuration
config.note: withDefault covers a missing value only; a malformed value still fails.

config-provider.title: Configuration supplied to tests
config-provider.note: Tests supply config without mutating the process environment.

managed-runtime.title: One runtime per process
managed-runtime.note: Build at module scope. Finalizers do not run when a serverless process is frozen; flush telemetry inside the invocation.

exhaustive-match.title: Exhaustive failure mapping
exhaustive-match.note: Adding a failure kind fails compilation until it is mapped.

log-annotations.title: Structured logs with annotations
log-annotations.note: Set request ids once; every log in the fiber carries them.

spans.title: Named spans on operations
spans.note: Effect.fn names the span and keeps stack frames. Spans are no-ops until a tracer is provided.

cause-aware-recovery.title: Recovery that lets interruption through
cause-aware-recovery.note: Catch causes only at supervision boundaries, and exclude interruption.

stream-paginate.title: Pagination as a stream
stream-paginate.note: A plain loop is clearer when it exits early or carries state.

bounded-concurrency.title: Bounded fan-out
bounded-concurrency.note: forEach is sequential by default; set concurrency from downstream capacity. A semaphore shares one limit across call sites.

partial-failure.title: Per-item outcomes
partial-failure.note: Collect each item's outcome instead of failing the batch.

request-batching.title: Batched lookups
request-batching.note: Earns its cost when many lookups happen in one tick.

clock.title: Injected time
clock.note: Code that reads Clock can be tested with TestClock.

test-clock.title: Virtual time in tests
test-clock.note: Requires the code under test to read Clock.

scoped-resource.title: Scoped acquire and release
scoped-resource.note: Release runs on success, failure and interruption.

cache.title: Cache with expiry and shared lookups
cache.note: Concurrent misses share one lookup; entries expire.

scoped-fiber.title: Owned background work
scoped-fiber.note: Work in a frozen serverless process does not continue; required work must finish before the handler returns or go to a queue.

test-layer.title: Test services through layers
test-layer.note: The code under test receives the double through its service, not a patched global.

rate-limit-schedule.title: Retry delay from rate-limit hints
rate-limit-schedule.note: Wait at least the provider's hint.

external-operation.title: One external-operation wrapper
external-operation.note: One wrapper gives every call a span, a deadline, a typed failure with operation and cause, and one retry owner.

replay-policy.title: Replay policy declared per operation
replay-policy.note: Each operation declares safe, token, observe or duplicate-tolerated. The executor retries only a transient failure of a replay-safe operation within the caller's budget. An observe operation returns an outcome-unknown failure the caller must handle.

failure-taxonomy.title: One failure classification
failure-taxonomy.note: One function maps provider status and codes to throttled, unavailable, unknown outcome, conflict, not found, forbidden, invalid and misconfigured.

entry-runner.title: One entry runner
entry-runner.note: One function per entry style derives the deadline from the platform, annotates logs, runs through the process runtime, and maps failures to responses.

config-module.title: One configuration module
config-module.note: Named getters for every key, with secrets redacted and parsing in one place.

error-family.title: Shared error family
error-family.note: One error shape for errors that share fields and purpose.

isolated-step.title: Named optional step
isolated-step.note: One combinator runs best-effort work under its own deadline, records the failure, and lets interruption through.

shared-schema.title: One schema per stored or exchanged shape
shared-schema.note: Readers and writers import the same schema.

cas-record.title: Conditional record store
cas-record.note: get returns value and version; create is if-absent; swap is if-version; each record stores its writer id so a lost-response retry recognizes its own write.

outbox.title: Effect ledger or outbox
outbox.note: Record the intended effect with the state change, perform it, record the result; delivery uses the record id as its dedupe key.

idempotent-entry.title: Idempotent entry
idempotent-entry.note: A dedupe record keyed by the event identity, with in-progress expiry from the platform deadline and the stored outcome.

observe-before-repeat.title: Observe before repeating
observe-before-repeat.note: After an unknown outcome, the operation's lookup finds the earlier effect before any new request.

shared-fake.title: Shared test doubles
shared-fake.note: One double per service, shared by every test, with real conflict and not-found behavior.

fault-injection.title: Fault-injecting doubles
fault-injection.note: Doubles that fail before applying, apply and lose the response, time out, or return stale data.

import-boundary.title: Import boundary rule
import-boundary.note: One adapter module owns the client; a lint rule such as no-restricted-imports with per-directory overrides lets only the adapter import it, so its deadline, typed failures and replay policy cannot be bypassed.

rules.mechanism: A change repeated without a dedupe key can apply twice when the first attempt succeeded but its response was lost.
rules.counter: The provider deduplicates by request content, or a repeat is harmless for this effect (a full overwrite with the same value).

rules.mechanism: A key generated per attempt or per process does not deduplicate a repeat from a new process or retry layer.
rules.counter: Every repeat happens in the same process, inside one call that reuses the key.

rules.mechanism: Retries at two layers multiply attempts and stretch past the caller's deadline.
rules.counter: The layers retry disjoint failure kinds and the total is bounded below the deadline.

rules.mechanism: A per-attempt timeout inside a retry does not bound the total; attempts and waits can exceed the caller's limit.
rules.counter: The retry count and waits are capped so the total stays under the caller's limit, and the cap is written down.

rules.mechanism: A network call inside a transaction holds locks for the call's latency, and a rollback cannot undo the remote effect.
rules.counter: The call is a read whose result must be consistent with the transaction and the store bounds transaction time.

rules.mechanism: A retry that never reads the provider's wait hint can retry before the provider allows, extending throttling.
rules.counter: The provider sends no wait hint for this operation, or the fixed delay already exceeds any hint it sends.

rules.mechanism: After a timeout on a change without a dedupe key, nothing finds out whether it happened.
rules.counter: The caller is a reconciler whose next pass observes state before acting.

rules.mechanism: An unbounded call holds the caller until the platform kills it, and the failure arrives without the operation's name.
rules.counter: An enclosing entry deadline interrupts this call and its abort signal reaches the transport.

rules.mechanism: A hand-written retry loop restates backoff, limits and jitter that a schedule declares once.
rules.counter: The loop does more than retry: it re-reads state, changes the request, or exits on a domain condition.

rules.mechanism: Retrying every failure alike repeats rejected and unknown-outcome failures that should stop or observe.
rules.counter: The only retry owner is a library that classifies failures itself, and the classification is cited.

rules.mechanism: A failure without the operation name and cause cannot be matched by callers or diagnosed from the log.
rules.counter: The failure is converted to a typed value one frame up, and that conversion is cited.

rules.mechanism: A failing call leaves no record of which operation failed or how long it took.
rules.counter: The call is on a hot path where a span costs more than it tells, and a coarser span covers it.

rules.mechanism: Fields read from an unvalidated response fail far from the call when the provider's shape changes.
rules.counter: A typed SDK owns the response shape and the code reads only fields it guarantees.

rules.mechanism: Each direct call restates deadline, failure typing and recording, and the copies drift.
rules.counter: The call is the wrapper's own implementation.

rules.mechanism: A client imported in several files has no single owner of its deadlines, failure typing and replay policy, and nothing stops a new file from importing it too.
rules.counter: The other importers are tests or scripts outside the shipped code.

rules.mechanism: Dependencies built per request repeat their setup cost and lose any cache or connection they hold.
rules.counter: The construction is a pure value with no setup cost, state or connection.

rules.mechanism: Work without a deadline from the platform limit is killed mid-effect instead of failing with a named outcome.
rules.counter: Every external call below the entry has its own deadline and their sum fits the platform limit.

rules.mechanism: Typed failures that fall into a generic response look like server faults to clients and hide permanent errors.
rules.counter: The entry is internal and its only consumer treats every failure the same.

rules.mechanism: Logs without the request id cannot be joined to the failing request.
rules.counter: The platform injects the request id into every log line already.

rules.mechanism: Fields read from raw input fail inside the work instead of as a named rejection.
rules.counter: A framework validator runs before the entry and its schema is cited.

rules.mechanism: A redelivered event repeats effects that the first delivery already applied.
rules.counter: Redelivery is disabled in the cited configuration, or every effect the entry applies is idempotent; cite each effect.

rules.mechanism: Providing layers inside each run rebuilds them per request.
rules.counter: The layers are constant values with no setup.

rules.mechanism: A secret that reaches a log, error or response is exposed to everyone who reads it.
rules.counter: The cited path masks the value before output.

rules.mechanism: A plain-string secret prints in full wherever it is logged or stringified.
rules.counter: The value is passed straight to a client constructor and never held elsewhere.

rules.mechanism: A missing value fails later, far from the key that caused it.
rules.counter: The key is optional and the code handles its absence explicitly.

rules.mechanism: Hand parsing accepts malformed values as NaN, false or partial objects.
rules.counter: The value is parsed once in a shared getter that reports a malformed value with the key name.

rules.mechanism: Each read of the same key restates its default, parsing and missing-value rule, and the copies drift.
rules.counter: Both reads go through one shared getter already.

rules.mechanism: Tests that mutate the process environment leak values between tests and cannot run in parallel.
rules.counter: The value is read at module load by code outside the project's control.

rules.mechanism: An error without a tag can be matched only by class or message, which breaks across module copies and rewording.
rules.counter: The error is thrown only to end the process and never matched.

rules.mechanism: A class instance written to storage or sent across a process loses its fields unless a schema encodes it.
rules.counter: Only its message string is written, by design.

rules.mechanism: An error without its cause hides the provider's code and request id from diagnosis.
rules.counter: It is raised for a condition with no underlying cause.

rules.mechanism: Matching on message text breaks when the text changes, and the compiler cannot see it.
rules.counter: The message is a provider's documented error code string.

rules.mechanism: Several error types with one shape and purpose make every consumer match each of them.
rules.counter: Consumers deliberately treat them differently, or their purposes differ.

rules.mechanism: A failure ended without a mark returns success for work that did not happen.
rules.counter: The swallowed work is best effort and the caller's result does not claim it.

rules.mechanism: Catching cancellation with failures turns a deadline or shutdown into success, and the enclosing work keeps running.
rules.counter: This is the outermost supervision boundary and it reports cancellation explicitly, or the caught cancellation is meant to end this work only.

rules.mechanism: Replacing a failure without its cause hides the original reason from logs and callers.
rules.counter: The cause contains a secret and is logged separately.

rules.mechanism: Recovery placed before a retry erases the failure the retry depends on, so the retry never runs.
rules.counter: The recovery is meant to stop retries for that failure kind and says so.

rules.mechanism: Each intended swallow restates its own deadline, log and cancellation handling.
rules.counter: It already uses the project's optional-step helper.

rules.mechanism: External data used without validation fails deep inside logic when its shape changes.
rules.counter: A typed SDK owns the shape and the code reads only fields it guarantees.

rules.mechanism: A cast on external data tells the compiler a shape no one checked.
rules.counter: The data was validated upstream and the validator is cited.

rules.mechanism: Two decoders of one shape drift; one accepts what the other rejects.
rules.counter: The two sites need different subsets on purpose.

rules.mechanism: A shape written and read by separate code drifts unless one schema owns both directions.
rules.counter: The writer is another system whose schema this code cannot share.

rules.mechanism: A corrupt record reported as a transport failure is retried as an outage instead of reaching a person.
rules.counter: Every consumer treats both the same by design.

rules.mechanism: Two writers that read, compute and write unconditionally overwrite each other's update.
rules.counter: A cited concurrency setting or lock serializes every writer of the record.

rules.mechanism: A retry after a committed write whose response was lost sees a conflict and treats its own write as another writer's.
rules.counter: The write is never retried.

rules.mechanism: A crash between the write and its paired effect loses or repeats the effect.
rules.counter: The effect is idempotent and a reconciler repeats it from the written state.

rules.mechanism: A read-modify-write with one code path is still lost when two requests or instances run it at once, unless a deployment setting prevents that.
rules.counter: The code's own structure, not deployment configuration, keeps the path from running twice at once.

rules.mechanism: An unbounded page walk grows with the data until it exceeds the deadline or memory.
rules.counter: The data set is bounded by a cited invariant.

rules.mechanism: One slow page holds the whole walk with no named failure.
rules.counter: An enclosing deadline covers the loop.

rules.mechanism: Each hand-written page loop restates token handling and termination.
rules.counter: Each loop's API differs in token shape so that one helper would need a callback per API.

rules.mechanism: Starting every item at once against a downstream service hits its rate limit or connection cap as the data grows.
rules.counter: The items are CPU-only work, or the downstream has no limit at the possible counts.

rules.mechanism: One item's failure abandons independent items that would have succeeded.
rules.counter: The caller retries the whole batch and every item is idempotent.

rules.mechanism: Item failures that are not reported make a partial result look complete.
rules.counter: The caller's result does not claim completeness.

rules.mechanism: One request per item multiplies latency and rate-limit cost where the provider accepts a list.
rules.counter: The batch API has different semantics or limits that the items exceed.

rules.mechanism: A timer race abandons the slower promise without cancelling it; the work continues unobserved.
rules.counter: The losing work holds no resource and has no effect.

rules.mechanism: A time-based decision without a test is exercised only in production.
rules.counter: The decision is a log timestamp or a trivial comparison.

rules.mechanism: Tests that wait real time are slow and flaky; patched globals leak between tests.
rules.counter: The code under test cannot read an injected clock and changing it is out of scope.

rules.mechanism: Wall-clock time can jump, so an elapsed check can fire early or never.
rules.counter: The duration is long and a clock jump only shifts it by a tolerated amount.

rules.mechanism: Free-text logs cannot be filtered or counted by event and field.
rules.counter: A developer-only debug line not shipped to production.

rules.mechanism: A log without the request id cannot be joined to the request that produced it.
rules.counter: A startup or process-wide log.

rules.mechanism: A logged secret or full payload is exposed to everyone with log access.
rules.counter: The value is masked before output, and the mask is cited.

rules.mechanism: An actionable failure below warning level is filtered out of alerts and level-filtered logs.
rules.counter: The failure is expected and handled, and this line is detail; or it is reported at the right level elsewhere.

rules.mechanism: An Effect log that is never yielded never runs, so the record is silently missing.
rules.counter: The Effect value is stored and run later, and the run is cited.

rules.mechanism: A resource released only on success leaks on failure, timeout or cancellation.
rules.counter: The process exits on every failure path, which releases it.

rules.mechanism: A process-lifetime resource held in a module variable has no owner that can rebuild or release it.
rules.counter: The resource is stateless and never needs release.

rules.mechanism: Two concurrent first callers each create the resource; one leaks or both are used.
rules.counter: The process handles one request at a time by configuration, or a duplicate is harmless.

rules.mechanism: A hand-built abort controller restates timer setup and cleanup that interruption provides.
rules.counter: The controller is owned by a framework boundary that passes the signal in.

rules.mechanism: A cache with no expiry or bound grows without limit and serves stale values.
rules.counter: The keys are a small fixed set and values never change.

rules.mechanism: Concurrent misses each start a lookup, multiplying load on the source at cold start.
rules.counter: The process handles one request at a time.

rules.mechanism: A cached failure keeps failing after the source recovers.
rules.counter: The failure is cached deliberately with a short expiry that is cited.

rules.mechanism: A source that changes while cached forever is never seen again by this process.
rules.counter: A change to the source does not affect correctness here, or the process lifetime is shorter than the change interval by a cited bound.

rules.mechanism: A write computed from a read taken before an await overwrites changes made during the await.
rules.counter: The process handles one request at a time and no timer touches the state.

rules.mechanism: Required work started without waiting is lost when the owner returns or the process freezes.
rules.counter: A durable queue or reconciler repeats the work.

rules.mechanism: A background failure that nothing observes never reaches a log or a caller.
rules.counter: A failure has nothing to report, such as a cache warm whose miss is retried on use.

rules.mechanism: Running an Effect inside Effect code starts a new runtime that loses the caller's interruption, context and span.
rules.counter: The nested run is inside a callback API that cannot take an Effect, and it receives the caller's signal.

rules.mechanism: Providing a layer on every call rebuilds it each time and breaks memoization.
rules.counter: The layer is a constant with no setup, and the call is a test.

rules.mechanism: A boundary that treats interruption and defects like typed failures reports a cancelled request as a server fault or a bug as a rejection.
rules.counter: The boundary only logs and rethrows.

rules.mechanism: A run without the caller's signal continues after the caller has given up.
rules.counter: The run is the process's main program.

rules.mechanism: A request-scoped value captured at layer build is shared by later requests.
rules.counter: The captured value is the same for every request.

rules.mechanism: Each copy of a double drifts from the others and from the real service.
rules.counter: The copies deliberately model different services.

rules.mechanism: A double installed by patching a global leaks between tests and hides the dependency from the code's interface.
rules.counter: The global belongs to third-party code with no seam.

rules.mechanism: A double that cannot apply-and-lose-the-response never exercises the replay path.
rules.counter: The code under test makes no change outside the process.

rules.mechanism: Real waits make tests slow and timing-dependent.
rules.counter: The wait is for a real external process in an integration test.
